existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: develops an African historical account of relational underdevelopment
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: Rodney’s checked excerpt supplies unequal power; Wallerstein’s 1986 reading distinguishes systemic constraint from simple stagnation. That sympathetic interpretation does not settle disputes over African agency or absorb all Rodney’s work into dependency theory.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: connects historical research with Pan-African politics and popular education
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: The Foundation describes dialogue with working people and Rastafarians in Jamaica, alongside scholarship and political activity. This is an institutional account of practice; the original Groundings text still needs a passage check.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Caribbean historical writing and London Marxist study inform Rodney’s formation
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: West’s assessment identifies The Black Jacobins. The Foundation names C. L. R. and Selma James in London study; James’s 1981 retrospective locates Rodney within a Caribbean intellectual inheritance. These sources support formation but not agreement on strategy or every textual debt.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: informs Rodney’s intellectual formation through Capitalism and Slavery
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: Michael West’s 2018 assessment reproduced by Verso names Capitalism and Slavery as formative. This remains a secondary attribution: no direct Rodney passage was located in this batch, and the two historical explanations are not identical.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Rodney contributes African research and a critique of underdevelopment through unequal power
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: The earlier Upper Guinea project adds regional research to the 1972 power argument and Ranger’s Dar recollection. Neither the thesis abstract nor the retrospective testimony verifies the full monograph; Dar es Salaam remains intellectually plural.
existing_incident_edges_inspected.map_label: Rodney: research, power and Dar es Salaam

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Rodney adapts materialist method to historical time and place
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: His 1975 lecture explicitly separates method from conclusions about nineteenth-century Europe. This is his account of a conceptual resource, not a claim that African/Caribbean history derives wholly from European theory.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Upper Guinea research connects regional change and Atlantic slave trading
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: The 1966 thesis abstract identifies European and intra-African forces; the 1970 book contributes regional scholarship. This does not certify every argument of the unread book or make Africans a single responding actor.
existing_incident_edges_inspected.map_label: Upper Guinea: regional and Atlantic relations

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Guyanese working people become subjects of differentiated labor history
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: The posthumous 1981 book addresses immigration, race, class, resistance and accommodation. Mapping it here identifies substantive social history, not membership in a unified school. Publisher-level support retains its limits.
existing_incident_edges_inspected.map_label: Guyana: labor, race and class divisions

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: James criticizes Rodney’s political preparation for taking power
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: The 1981 memorial lecture offers a strategic disagreement alongside admiration. James’s diagnosis is not adopted as an explanation of the assassination or proof of what Rodney did not know. This differs from the formative influence in edge_156.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Names Rodney’s How Europe Underdeveloped Africa as a model that drew him toward historical and revolutionary study.
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: In his own named-resources answer, Kelley describes Rodney’s book as opening dependency/underdevelopment literature, then places it with Du Bois and James among three formative historical texts. Samir Amin and Andre Gunder Frank retain credit in that pathway. Original Rodney book remains unread for this dossier; retrospective self-report is not an exclusive genealogy.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Roediger singles out Rodney’s Guyanese working-class history as a model for studying race and labor across Atlantic economies.
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: Own 1993, 143/n40 strongly praises A History of Guyanese Working People 1881–1905, Baltimore/London 1981 manifestation, in explicit transnational extension alongside Linebaugh/Fryer. Note citation is a substantive exemplar, no personal mentorship, original book read or automatic James/Thompson influence from Linebaugh title.

named_group_routes_inspected.relationship: James, Williams and Césaire challenge different imperial historical narratives
named_group_routes_inspected.evidence_note: James, Williams, and Rodney challenge different imperial narratives; national liberation is not a single explanatory position. Césaire’s checked opening attacks civilizing claims; Williams’s economic propositions remain disputed.

named_group_routes_inspected.relationship: extends analysis to unequal international relations
named_group_routes_inspected.evidence_note: Williams and Rodney make empire, slavery, and unequal development historical problems. This does not derive all dependency theory from a generic field. Frank’s notes add particular Latin American histories, including Furtado and Góngora, used selectively rather than as a generic economics origin.

named_group_routes_inspected.relationship: Rodney and Williams connect empire with distinct explanations of unequal economic change
named_group_routes_inspected.evidence_note: Rodney and Williams provide distinct arguments concerning empire and economic change; neither stands for every dependency theorist. Rodney’s primary excerpt emphasizes power and control; its broad loss-of-agency rhetoric remains his argument.
named_group_routes_inspected.map_label: Rodney’s power relations; Williams’s slavery debate

named_group_routes_inspected.relationship: Frank and Wallerstein challenge national-stage explanations of underdevelopment
named_group_routes_inspected.evidence_note: Relational underdevelopment contests a picture of independent national stages; dependency arguments themselves differ. Frank’s sections I–IX reject a prior-stage/dual-society explanation; Wallerstein p. 389 directly names Rostow, but retains stages of systems. This target does not describe every modernization theorist or abolish all historical sequencing.

named_group_routes_inspected.relationship: Liberation politics and critiques of colonial knowledge contribute to distinct African historical projects
named_group_routes_inspected.evidence_note: Decolonization supplies important contexts, not a sole origin of African historiography. Ki-Zerbo’s opening calls for critical reconstruction rather than reversing inherited myths; Ranger recalls institutional variety.

named_group_routes_inspected.relationship: Rodney connects African history to an account of underdevelopment structured by unequal power
named_group_routes_inspected.evidence_note: Rodney’s work replaces Vansina as the pertinent theoretical reference; the field is broader than dependency analysis. The primary excerpt strengthens the argument check; neither its generalizations nor dependency theory define the field.

Veracini dates a usage, until the late 1970s, naming a diehard hyper-colonialism challenged by anti-colonial insurgencies. Mamdani revisits the first postcolonial generation's political economy (Rodney) to ask how settler and native became political identities. Comparison: no line of descent from liberation politics to the later field is asserted. Addendum 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md P.6, p4B_rel_13): Veracini 2011, pp. 5–7 (read in full), 'Decolonisation is not settler decolonisation': 'arguing against colonialism is not the same thing as condemning settler colonialism'; 'if colonialism ends with the coloniser's departure … settler colonialism ends with an indigenous ultimate permanence'. Tuck and Yang 2012, p. 31 (read): 'Decolonization is not equivocal to other anti-colonial struggles. It is incommensurable.' Both keep the two decolonisations apart, which is why a comparison and not a descent is drawn.

named_group_routes_inspected.relationship: Credits Black Reconstruction as one of the formative historical models that drew him into the discipline.
named_group_routes_inspected.evidence_note: Kelley explicitly names Du Bois’s book alongside James’s Black Jacobins and Rodney’s How Europe Underdeveloped Africa. The three are co-credited; this is stronger than a shared Black-history topic or bibliographic mention. The original Du Bois book remains unread here.
